So far as I understand, a treaty made by the United States government becomes to all intents and purposes public property when it goes to the Senate. I may be mistaken in that. The Senate, I believe, does sometimes deal with treaties in secret session, when of course they are not matters of public property. I do not know how it may be in the present instance. What I object to is that the terms of this treaty should have been made the property of the people of the United States and of their legislature and should not at the same time have

been made the property of the people of Canada and of this parliament. There may be diplomatic difficulties in the way, I do not know about that. All I desire to do is to emphasize, subect to any superior knowledge of those difficulties which the Prime Minister may have, my belief that that treaty, when placed before the Congress and the people of the United States, ought at the same time to be placed before the parliament and the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that I have any other knowledge on this subject than is common to everybody. I am not prepared to controvert the statement made by my hon. friend, that the moment a treaty is submitted to the American Senate it becomes public property in the United States. My impression is-I speak subject to correction, and I would like to have the point cleared up between now and to-morrow-that the treaty is communicated to the Senate, but not to the House of Representatives. As to that, I will make inquiries. So far as we are concerned, my hon. friend knows that a treaty is not communicated to parliament unless and until it is ratified by the King. That is the etiquette of our system, and that is the only reason why this treaty has not been communicated to parliament. I know that there is a good deal of inconvenience felt on this side of the Atlantic for the very reason stated by my hon. friend. I believe that in the United States a treaty may be given to the press some time before it is given to the Senate. We do not admit anything of that kind in this country, as my hon. friend knows, and it is simply because in this matter we follow the traditions of British diplomacy, under which parliament does not receive the treaty until it has been signed by His Majesty the King. But I quite agree with my hon. friend that it is inconvenient that we should not have the matter made public in this country as soon as it is in the United States.

Of course, we are all quite familiar with the doctrine which the Prime Minister has laid down very correctly, that the treaty-making power under our constitutional usage resides in the King. But he may exercise that power by entering into a convention subject to the consent of the Imperial Parliament or the parliament of any great dependency of the empire. I think that course was pursued, if my memory serves me correctly, in the case of the French treaty. No doubt in that case another reason prevailed, namely, that the treaty could not become operative without an enactment of this parliament. But apart from that altogether, it might perhaps be desirable to consider whether or not a treaty such as that recently negotiated should not be framed in' Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
the same terms, especially when it is a treaty concluded between His Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada and the people of the United States, whose treaties do not become valid and binding upon them until they have been ratified by the Senate. I do not know whether I make myself clear to my hon. friend. A treaty which we make with the United States is not valid or binding upon them until it is ratified by their Senate. It might be worth considering whether or not our treaties dealing with important subjects should not have a clause to the effect that they should not become binding on His Majesty until they have been ratified by the parliament of Canada. I hope my right hon. friend will take that into consideration. It seems to me that it might very well be taken into consideration, and it might possibly lead to a different mode of conducting these treaties than that which has prevailed in the past.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no exception to take to the suggestion made by my hon. friend. On the contrary, I am quite disposed to agree with everything he says. I would go further. Even admitting that the King alone has the treaty-making power, I see no reason why, the moment a treaty is signed by the parties who negotiated it, it should not be given to the public even before it is ratified by His Majesty. Although the present treaty has been signed, I may say we have not yet received an official copy of it.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 3.50 p.m.
Wednesday, January 27, 1909.
